entries.sentence: The NHS describes Alzheimer's disease as gradual, with symptoms that develop over many years and eventually become more severe.
entries.note: NHS summary: symptoms develop gradually over many years and become more severe

entries.sentence: In the early stage, small memory problems are usually the first sign, such as forgetting recent conversations or events, misplacing items or struggling to think of the right word.
entries.note: NHS: memory lapses main early symptom; forgetting recent conversations/events, misplacing items, trouble thinking of right word

entries.sentence: Anxiety, mood changes or periods of confusion can appear too, and some people have trouble judging distances or get lost in familiar places.
entries.note: NHS: mood changes, anxiety, confusion; distance judgement/getting lost from Alzheimer's Society factsheet (summary blended)

entries.sentence: In the middle stage, memory problems get worse, and a person may find it hard to remember the names of people they know or to recognise family and friends.
entries.note: NHS: middle stage worsening memory, names, recognising family and friends

entries.sentence: Disturbed sleep, delusions and changes in mood can also occur, and by this point someone usually needs support with everyday living.
entries.note: NHS: disturbed sleep, delusions, mood changes; usually needs support with everyday living

entries.sentence: In the later stage, symptoms become much more severe, with difficulty eating and swallowing, trouble moving without help, weight loss, incontinence and gradual loss of speech.
entries.note: NHS lists these later-stage features

entries.sentence: Alzheimer's is the most common form of dementia, and other common types include vascular dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies and frontotemporal dementia.
entries.note: Alzheimer's Society types page: Alzheimer's most common; vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal

entries.sentence: When someone has more than one type it is called mixed dementia, and the most common mix is Alzheimer's disease with vascular dementia.
entries.note: Summary: mixed dementia; most common is Alzheimer's plus vascular

entries.sentence: Young-onset dementia is dementia that begins before the age of 65.
entries.note: Summary: UK source defines young-onset as before age 65 (URL attribution to types page uncertain)

entries.sentence: Mild cognitive impairment involves minor problems with memory or thinking, and it is not a type of dementia, but a person with it is more likely to go on to develop dementia.
entries.note: Summary: MCI minor cognition problems, not a type of dementia, more likely to develop dementia (page attribution uncertain; Alzheimer's Society MCI pages)

entries.sentence: Memory problems are not always caused by dementia, because depression, stress, medicines, and alcohol or drugs can all cause them.
entries.note: NHS diagnosis: GP can rule out other causes; depression, stress, medicines, alcohol or drugs

entries.sentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP if you are worried about your memory or think you may have dementia.
entries.note: NHS: best to see a GP if worried about memory

entries.sentence: At the appointment the GP will ask about your concerns and what you or your family have noticed.
entries.note: NHS: GP asks about concerns and what you/family noticed

entries.sentence: You will typically be asked some questions and given memory, thinking and pen-and-paper tasks.
entries.note: NHS: questions and memory/thinking/pen and paper tasks

entries.sentence: If needed, the GP can refer you to a specialist, often at a memory clinic or memory service.
entries.note: NHS: GP can refer to specialist; memory clinic/service is where detailed assessment usually happens (summary)

entries.sentence: These teams may include neurologists, who review brain scans, and neuropsychologists, who carry out tests of memory and thinking.
entries.note: NIA/summary: memory clinics include neurologists and neuropsychologists

entries.sentence: Blood and other standard tests may also be done to look for other possible causes.
entries.note: Summary: blood and other standard tests may be ordered to identify other possible causes

entries.sentence: Not everyone needs a brain scan, but for many people a CT, MRI or PET scan gives useful information, and an MRI can show which parts of the brain are shrinking.
entries.note: NIA: scan not always necessary, can help; MRI shows shrinking parts

entries.sentence: There is no single simple and reliable test, so diagnosis relies on combining history, cognitive testing and sometimes scans.
entries.note: Summary: no simple reliable single test; combine history, cognitive tests, imaging

entries.sentence: The Alzheimer's Society suggests it may help to bring someone along to appointments.
entries.note: Summary: Alzheimer's Society practical tip (URL is the diagnosing-dementia guide, not in refs; attributed loosely to NHS page)

entries.sentence: The NHS says there is no cure for Alzheimer's disease, but some medicines can temporarily ease symptoms or, for some people, slow progression.
entries.note: NHS treatment page summary

entries.sentence: Donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine can be prescribed for early to mid-stage disease, and memantine is used for moderate or severe disease.
entries.note: NHS treatment summary

entries.sentence: Non-drug options include cognitive stimulation therapy, which uses group activities and exercises to build memory and problem-solving skills.
entries.note: NHS treatment summary

entries.sentence: Cognitive rehabilitation involves a trained professional helping the person work towards a personal goal.
entries.note: NHS treatment summary

entries.sentence: Reminiscence and life story work draw on photos, music and keepsakes.
entries.note: NHS treatment summary

entries.sentence: When someone has persistent aggression or extreme distress after other coping strategies have failed, a consultant psychiatrist can prescribe an antipsychotic such as risperidone, which has serious side effects and should be used for as short a time as possible.
entries.note: NHS summary: risperidone for persistent aggression/extreme distress once strategies failed; lowest dose, shortest time, serious side effects

entries.sentence: NICE has so far not recommended the newer medicines lecanemab and donanemab for routine NHS use, saying they are not currently cost effective, so the NICE website has the current position.
entries.note: NICE news titles/summary 2024-2025; could not confirm if later reversed

entries.sentence: NHS guidance encourages staying socially active, for example through dementia-friendly groups or memory cafes where people swap practical tips.
entries.note: Summary of NHS and NHS inform living-well pages

entries.sentence: A steady daily routine is recommended, and it can encourage feelings of security and worth.
entries.note: Summary: routine recommended; one source says security and worth

entries.sentence: Memory aids around the home can help, such as pictures on cupboard doors showing what is inside, and reminder devices or appointment alerts.
entries.note: Summary: memory aids, pictures on cupboard doors, reminder devices and alerts

entries.sentence: General health advice covers diet, exercise, sleep, and regular dental, eyesight and hearing checks.
entries.note: Summary of NHS living well advice

entries.sentence: Depression is very common in dementia, and a GP can talk through talking treatments that can help.
entries.note: Summary: depression very common; talk to GP; talking treatments

entries.sentence: You can ask your local council for a needs assessment, and carers can ask for a carer's assessment.
entries.note: Summary: council needs assessment; carer's assessment available

entries.sentence: NHS England describes advance care planning as fundamental for everyone living with dementia, and it can include choosing someone you trust to act for you through a Lasting Power of Attorney.
entries.note: Summary: NHS England advance care planning fundamental; LPA (URL for NHS England page was in results but not recorded here; attribution loose)

entries.sentence: The outlook varies considerably from person to person.
entries.note: Summary: outlook varies considerably

entries.sentence: The Alzheimer's Society says the middle stage is often the longest, while the later stage is usually the shortest.
entries.note: Summary of Alzheimer's Society factsheet 458 (numbers omitted)

entries.sentence: In the later stage many people have trouble eating or swallowing, which can lead to choking, chest infections and other problems.
entries.note: NHS summary

entries.sentence: Delirium is a sudden change in mental state, where the person seems not themselves, and it is different from the slow worsening of dementia.
entries.note: Summary: delirium sudden change; dementia develops slowly

entries.sentence: Causes of sudden confusion include a urinary tract infection, a stroke, low blood sugar and a head injury.
entries.note: NHS confusion page summary

entries.sentence: A urinary infection in a person with dementia can cause sudden and severe confusion.
entries.note: Alzheimer's Society UTI page: UTI can cause sudden severe confusion/delirium

entries.sentence: The NHS says to go to A&E or call 999 if someone suddenly becomes confused, and the Alzheimer's Society advises seeking help straight away from the GP or NHS 111 if you think a person with dementia has delirium.
entries.note: Summary: NHS A&E/999 for sudden confusion; Alzheimer's Society GP or NHS 111 for suspected delirium. Two routes differ; both stated

entries.sentence: Dementia is the biggest single risk factor for delirium, so a change in behaviour may be missed or put down to dementia.
entries.note: Summary of delirium sources

entries.sentence: Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia, but it is not the only one.
entries.note: Alzheimer's Society types

entries.sentence: Other common types include vascular dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies and frontotemporal dementia.
entries.note: types page

entries.sentence: Some people have more than one type, which is called mixed dementia, and the most common mix is Alzheimer's disease with vascular dementia.
entries.note: types page summary

entries.sentence: The NHS says there is no cure, but some medicines can temporarily ease symptoms or, for some people, slow progression.
entries.note: NHS treatment summary

entries.sentence: Non-drug approaches such as cognitive stimulation therapy and reminiscence work are also used.
entries.note: NHS treatment summary

entries.sentence: Local councils can offer a needs assessment, and carers can ask for a carer's assessment.
entries.note: living-well summary

entries.sentence: Not everyone does, because a brain scan is not always necessary.
entries.note: NIA summary

entries.sentence: For many people a CT, MRI or PET scan can give useful information, either to support a diagnosis of Alzheimer's or to rule out other causes.
entries.note: NIA summary

entries.sentence: A scan can also look normal in the early stage, when changes may not yet show.
entries.note: NIA summary

entries.sentence: A sudden change is different from the slow worsening of dementia and may be delirium.
entries.note: summary

entries.sentence: Causes include a urinary tract infection, a stroke, low blood sugar and a head injury.
entries.note: NHS confusion

entries.note: summary; two routes stated

entries.sentence: The Alzheimer's Society suggests that it may be helpful to bring someone else along.
entries.note: Summary: Alzheimer's Society tip; loosely attributed

entries.sentence: The GP will ask what you or your family have noticed, and may ask you some questions and set memory and thinking tasks.
entries.note: NHS diagnosis page

entries.note: NHS diagnosis: GP can rule out other causes

entries.sentence: Gradual, with symptoms developing over many years.
entries.note: NHS

entries.note: NHS

entries.sentence: Alzheimer's disease.
entries.note: Alzheimer's Society types

entries.note: NHS treatment

entries.sentence: Cognitive stimulation therapy, cognitive rehabilitation and reminiscence work.
entries.note: NHS treatment

entries.note: summary; two routes

entries.sentence: See a GP about memory concerns.
